track.name: langchain-rag
track.label: LangChain & RAG Basics
track.summary: Go from raw API calls to production-ready retrieval-augmented generation systems. Learn LangChain, vector databases, RAG pipelines, and LangChain agents with Python.

phases.title: LLM APIs
phases.description: Call the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs directly from Python, understand tokens and costs, and learn the Python basics needed to work with LLM responses.

phases.title: LangChain Fundamentals
phases.description: Use LangChain's chains, prompt templates, LLM wrappers, memory modules, and document loaders to build structured LLM applications.

phases.title: Vector Databases & Embeddings
phases.description: Understand what vector embeddings are, store them in FAISS and Chroma, and run similarity searches to retrieve semantically relevant content.

phases.title: RAG Pipeline
phases.description: Build a complete retrieval-augmented generation pipeline end-to-end, covering document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, and answer generation.

phases.title: Agents & Tools
phases.description: Build LangChain ReAct agents that call tools, use function calling, and execute multi-step research tasks autonomously.

phases.title: Deployment & Production
phases.description: Ship a working demo with Streamlit, trace and debug with LangSmith, and put in place cost-monitoring and reliability practices.

topics.title: OpenAI API Quickstart
topics.description: Install the OpenAI Python SDK, authenticate with an API key, and send your first chat-completion request from a Python script.

steps.d: Run pip install openai and confirm with python -c 'import openai; print(openai.__version__)'.
Generate an OpenAI API key in your account dashboard, set it as OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable, and verify with a test call.
Create a Python script that calls openai.ChatCompletion.create() with model='gpt-4o-mini', prompt='Hello', and captures the response.
Extract the content from response.choices[0].message.content, print it, and verify you received the model's reply.
Run 3-5 different prompts through your script (question, code request, concept description) and observe how responses change.

topics.title: Anthropic Claude API
topics.description: Call the Anthropic API using the Python SDK, explore available Claude models, and compare response formats with OpenAI's output.

steps.d: Run pip install anthropic and verify with python -c 'import anthropic; print(anthropic.__version__)'.
Get an API key from console.anthropic.com, set it as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable, and test the connection.
Create a Python script using client = anthropic.Anthropic() and call client.messages.create() with model='claude-3-5-sonnet', then extract the text response.
Ask the same prompt to both APIs (e.g. 'Explain quantum computing') and write a one-sentence comparison of tone, detail, or style.
Pass a multi-paragraph document as the user message and observe Claude's ability to reference information from it.

topics.title: Tokens, Costs, and Python Basics
topics.description: Learn how tokenisation works, estimate API costs before running large jobs, and write the minimal Python (loops, dicts, files) needed for LLM scripts.

steps.d: Go to https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer, paste a paragraph of text, and note how many tokens it contains.
Calculate: if your batch has 1000 documents of 500 tokens each at $0.03 per 1K input tokens, what's the total cost?
Create a Python script that takes a prompt, counts tokens with tiktoken, multiplies by OpenAI's pricing, and prints estimated cost.
Make an OpenAI API call, inspect response.usage to extract prompt_tokens and completion_tokens, and print them to verify token counts.
Modify your first API script to write responses to a file as JSON so you can review them without re-calling the API.

topics.title: Chains and Prompt Templates
topics.description: Use LangChain's PromptTemplate and LLMChain to compose reusable, parameterised prompts and pipe them through an LLM in a single call.

steps.d: In LangChain, write PromptTemplate(input_variables=['topic', 'tone'], template='Write about {topic} in a {tone} style') and test with two topics.
Create an LLMChain that pipes your template through an OpenAI or Claude LLM using ChatOpenAI() or ChatAnthropic().
Call chain.run(topic='AI safety', tone='beginner-friendly') and verify the output matches your template and LLM choice.
Add an output parser such as StrOutputParser or JsonOutputParser to ensure responses are formatted as expected.
Run your chain 5 times and time each call, then review outputs for consistency and accuracy.

topics.title: Memory and Conversation History
topics.description: Add conversation memory to your chains so the LLM can reference prior turns, and choose the right memory type for your context-length budget.

steps.d: Import ConversationBufferMemory and pass it to your LLMChain so the LLM remembers all prior messages.
Run a conversation where you ask a question, then a follow-up that references the first message, and verify the LLM tracks context.
Replace ConversationBufferMemory with ConversationSummaryMemory to summarise old messages and keep the conversation window manageable.
Measure context-window usage with buffer vs. summary memory for a 10-turn conversation and note the token savings.
Build a conversational chatbot on a real task (e.g. customer service, technical support) and verify it maintains context across 20+ turns.

topics.title: Document Loaders and Text Splitters
topics.description: Load PDFs, web pages, and text files into LangChain, split them into manageable chunks, and prepare them for embedding.

steps.d: Use PyPDFLoader to load a multi-page PDF (e.g. research paper) and print the first page text to verify it loaded correctly.
Use RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size=1000 to split the PDF into pieces and count how many chunks you got.
Use WebBaseLoader to fetch a URL, then split the HTML content into chunks using the same splitter.
Split the same document with three different chunk sizes (500, 1000, 2000) and observe how chunk count changes.
Load, split, and format a document so each chunk is ready to pass to an embedding model without extra preprocessing.

topics.title: What Are Vector Embeddings?
topics.description: Understand how text is converted to high-dimensional vectors, what semantic similarity means numerically, and why embeddings power modern search.

steps.d: Use OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small to embed five short sentences and inspect the resulting vectors' dimensions (should be 1536).
Embed two similar sentences (e.g. 'The cat sat on the mat' and 'A cat rested on a mat'), compute cosine similarity, and confirm score is close to 1.0.
Take one 1000-token chunk from a document, embed it, and store the resulting vector alongside the text.
Embed the same text with text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large, then note differences in vector size and latency.
Embed the same sentence with text-embedding-3-small (1536-dim) and text-embedding-3-large (3072-dim), print each vector's length, then compute cosine similarity between the two embeddings.

topics.title: Setting Up FAISS and Chroma
topics.description: Index a document collection in FAISS (in-memory) and Chroma (persistent), and compare their trade-offs for development versus production.

steps.d: Use LangChain's FAISS.from_documents() to index 5-10 chunks and save the index with .save_local('my_index').
Query your index with similarity_search('What is machine learning?', k=3) and review the top 3 results.
Install Chroma with from_documents(), load the same chunks, and run the same similarity search to compare results.
Time a similarity search in both FAISS and Chroma and note which is faster and whether Chroma's persistence justifies the difference.
Write one sentence explaining whether you'd use FAISS or Chroma for a prototype RAG system and why.

topics.title: Similarity Search in Practice
topics.description: Run k-nearest-neighbour queries against a vector store, tune top-k and score thresholds, and inspect retrieved chunks for relevance.

steps.d: Query your vector store with top_k=5 to retrieve the 5 most relevant chunks for a query and list the relevance scores.
Filter results to only return chunks with similarity score > 0.75 and compare how many results you get vs. k=5 without filtering.
Run 3 different queries on your vector store and for each, print the full text of the top result to judge relevance manually.
Query 10 times and manually rate each result as 'Relevant', 'Partially relevant', or 'Irrelevant', then calculate precision and recall.
Test different combinations of top_k (3, 5, 10) and similarity thresholds (0.6, 0.75, 0.9) to find the best balance.

topics.title: RAG Architecture End-to-End
topics.description: Wire together document loading, embedding, vector storage, retrieval, and answer generation into a complete RAG pipeline.

steps.d: Create a pipeline: load a PDF → split into chunks → embed each chunk → store in a vector database.
Wrap your vector store in LangChain's as_retriever(search_type='similarity', search_kwargs={'k': 3}) to make it queryable.
Create a prompt template that takes {context} and {question} and formats them as 'Use the following context to answer the question.'
Create a RAGChain that retrieves context for a question, then pipes it with the question through your prompt to an LLM.
Ask your RAG chain a question about your document and verify the answer is grounded in the retrieved context.

topics.title: Chunking Strategies
topics.description: Compare fixed-size, recursive, semantic, and sentence-window chunking strategies and measure how each affects retrieval quality.

steps.d: Use CharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200) and count resulting chunks for a 10,000-word document.
Use RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with the same size and compare chunk quality (semantic boundaries vs. hard breaks).
Manually write a splitter that groups sentences into chunks of 500 tokens each while preserving sentence boundaries.
Index the same document with fixed, recursive, and sentence-window chunking, run 5 queries on each, and compare retrieval quality.
Write one sentence explaining which chunking strategy you'd use for a production RAG system and why.

topics.title: Reranking and Retrieval Optimization
topics.description: Apply a cross-encoder reranker after initial retrieval, use MMR for diversity, and evaluate the pipeline with simple hit-rate metrics.

steps.d: Use BM25Retriever from LangChain to retrieve relevant chunks without embeddings and compare speed vs. semantic search.
After initial retrieval, use a cross-encoder reranker (e.g., sentence-transformers) to rescore top-k results.
Use search_type='mmr' to retrieve diverse chunks that avoid redundancy, then compare results to standard similarity search.
Run 10 test queries and measure retrieval precision (how many top-3 are relevant) and average latency.
Combine BM25 for speed, a reranker for quality, and MMR for diversity, then measure final pipeline latency and precision.

topics.title: ReAct Agents in LangChain
topics.description: Build a ReAct agent that alternates reasoning steps with tool calls, observe the Thought/Action/Observation loop in LangChain's executor.

steps.d: Use LangChain's create_react_agent with a tool such as Google search and run it on a multi-step question.
Run your agent and print the output, then mark each Thought, Action, and Observation to see how many reasoning steps it took.
Define a Python function like `multiply(a, b)` and wrap it as a LangChain Tool to use in your agent.
Add your RAG retriever as a tool the agent can call, enabling it to fetch relevant documents during reasoning.
Ask your agent a complex question requiring reasoning and tool calls (e.g. 'What are the top 3 risks in this document?').

topics.title: Tool-Calling and Function Calling
topics.description: Define Python functions as LangChain tools, bind them to an LLM with function calling, and handle structured output reliably.

steps.d: Write a simple function like def get_user(user_id) that returns user data, then wrap it with @tool decorator.
Use model.bind_tools([get_user]) to enable Claude or GPT to call the function by requesting a tool call.
Write a loop that calls the LLM, checks if it requests a tool call, executes your function, and feeds the result back.
Configure your tool-calling prompt to request JSON responses (e.g. {'type': 'get_user', 'user_id': 123}) and parse them.
Create three tools (e.g. get_user, search, send_email) and chain them so the agent can call any combination to complete a task.

topics.title: Building a Simple Research Agent
topics.description: Create an agent that can search the web, read pages, and synthesise an answer to a research question using a chain of tool calls.

steps.d: Wrap a web search API (Google Custom Search, SerpAPI) as a LangChain tool that takes a query and returns URLs and titles.
Create a tool that fetches full content from a URL and retrieves semantically related chunks from a vector store.
Create an agent with search and retrieval tools that breaks down a research question into sub-questions and gathers evidence.
After the agent completes searches and retrievals, prompt it to write a final answer that cites specific sources.
Ask your agent a real research question (e.g. 'Latest quantum error correction developments?') and verify it finds recent sources.

topics.title: Streamlit for LLM Demos
topics.description: Build an interactive web UI for your RAG pipeline using Streamlit — add a chat interface, file upload, and source citations in under 100 lines.

steps.d: Run pip install streamlit, then create app.py with import streamlit as st and verify with streamlit run app.py.
Add st.chat_message() and st.chat_input() to create a conversational interface where users can type questions.
Link your Streamlit chat input to your RAG chain so each user question triggers retrieval and generation.
Add code to display retrieved chunks alongside the AI response so users can see what documents the answer came from.
Use st.file_uploader() to let users upload PDFs, split and embed them in real-time, then search their uploaded files.

topics.title: LangSmith Tracing and Debugging
topics.description: Connect LangSmith to your LangChain application, trace every chain run, inspect intermediate steps, and compare prompt versions.

steps.d: Sign up at smith.langchain.com, create an API key, and set LANGCHAIN_API_KEY and LANGCHAIN_PROJECT environment variables.
Set os.environ['LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2'] = 'true', then run your chain and watch traces appear in LangSmith.
Open LangSmith, find your recent run, and click through to see input, output, and latency for each step in your chain.
Modify your prompt, give it a new version name in LangSmith, and compare outputs side-by-side for the same test queries.
Open a run in LangSmith, click 'Share', and send the link to a colleague to review your chain's performance together.

topics.title: Cost Monitoring and Optimization
topics.description: Track token usage and API spend, apply prompt caching and model-selection strategies, and set budget guardrails for production workloads.

steps.d: Add code to log token counts from each API call and multiply by per-token pricing to track real-time spend.
Log into https://platform.openai.com/usage weekly and record your spend against your budget.
Calculate: if your RAG runs 100 queries/day with 1000 input tokens and 200 output tokens each, what's the monthly cost?
Implement one optimization: use a cheaper model (gpt-4o-mini instead of gpt-4), cache embeddings, or batch requests.
Implement code that pauses your system if hourly or daily spend exceeds a threshold you define, preventing runaway costs.
